questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator says "ckyd cp x;k" (the boy ran away) at the end of the first story, linking it to the boy's answer "eSa ;koTtUe yksdlsok d:¡ xk".
questions.a: The boy's answer — "I want to become a servant of the country" — rejects the inspector's colonial framework (which expected a career like clerk or lawyer) and the father's material aspirations. The narrator uses "cp x;k" metaphorically: the boy escapes the predefined roles. A student who says "he physically ran out of the room" misses the symbolic escape and shows literal-level comprehension only.

questions.q: In "?kM+h osQ iq”ksZ", the author lists astronomers, historians, and geographers as "osn'kkL=kK èkekZpk;ks±". Apply the concept of 'personification of epistemology' to explain what each group represents in the debate on time.
questions.a: Astronomers represent cyclic, measurable time (planetary motion); historians represent linear, event-driven time (cause-effect); geographers represent spatialized time (distance/travel). A wrong assignment (e.g., "historians measure seconds") shows the student cannot map abstract disciplines to their temporal metaphors, a skill needed for Board's long-answer questions on this essay.

questions.q: Compare the function of the father in "ckyd cp x;k" with the function of the gardener (mali) in "<sys pqu yks". How do both characters mediate between the protagonist and society's expectations?
questions.a: The father enforces societal expectations (colonial career, obedience) through violence; the gardener presents nature's neutral bounty (three fruits) and lets the chooser decide. Both are gatekeepers, but the father closes options while the gardener opens them. A student who only describes their actions (slapping vs offering fruit) without analyzing their structural role as "mediators of expectation" fails the analytical demand.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to make the three fruits in "<sys pqu yks" speak in first person. Does this strengthen or weaken the allegory? Justify with two textual reasons.
questions.a: It strengthens the allegory because (1) each fruit articulates its own philosophy directly (power, knowledge, pleasure) without narrator filtration, making the debate immediate; (2) the first-person voices create dramatic tension when the chooser must reject two. A student who says "it's just a story device" cannot defend the artistic choice, a common Board competency trap.

questions.q: Create a one-paragraph ending for "ckyd cp x;k" where the boy meets the inspector again ten years later. The boy must speak in a way that echoes his original answer "eSa ;koTtUe yksdlsok d:¡ xk" but shows growth. Write the dialogue only.
questions.a: A strong answer will have the boy reference his past words, show concrete service (teaching, healing, organizing), and retain the idealistic core while acknowledging complexity. A weak answer merely repeats the original line or makes the boy a high-ranking officer, missing the nuance that "yksdlsok" (servant of people) is not a job title but a stance.
